Effect of COVID-19 Lockdown on Air Pollutant Levels in California

The COVID-19 pandemic prompted an unprecedented societal response. On March 19, 2020, California became the first U.S. state to issue a mandatory stay-at-home order, significantly reducing traffic, industrial and human activity. This created a rare natural experiment: the opportunity to isolate and measure the short-term effect of reduced human activity on air quality and whether lockdown policies will have a positive effect in controlling greenhouse gas emissions.

This project explores how California's lockdown affected concentrations of five key air pollutants: CO, NO₂, O₃, PM₂.₅, and PM₁₀, using 2019 as a pre-pandemic baseline for year-over-year comparison.

5 Pollutants
3 Years
25+ Counties
56,518 Observations
Mar 19 Lockdown date

Results reflect county-level monitoring data. See Limitations.

01 / Method

Methods

This was a year-over-year comparison: 2019 served as the baseline representing normal air quality data while 2020 was the treatment year. This controlled for seasonality without requiring a regression model.

The analysis was conducted in three phases:

Phase 1 / Data wrangling

See complete data wrangling conducted in the Jupyter Notebook.

Phase 2 / Results and exploratory data analysis

Monthly mean concentrations were calculated for each of the five key pollutants. The lockdown period (March 19 to June 30, 2020) was defined as the comparison window. Percentage change relative to 2019 was calculated for each pollutant during this window.

Phase 3 / Discussion and limitations

Primary traffic-related pollutants (NO₂, CO) were expected to respond readily to lockdown. PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ results were examined separately due to their unusual rise in late 2020.

02 / Results

Statewide trends and county-level reductions

Figure 1. Month-by-month pollutant comparison: 2019 vs. 2020 vs. 2021

Figure 1 · Month-by-month pollutant comparison: 2019 vs. 2020 vs. 2021 · statewide monthly means

Monthly averages across all five pollutants and counties revealed consistent year-over-year patterns for CO, NO₂, and O₃, with 2020 values dropping slightly below 2019 levels during the lockdown period. The clearest divergence appears in PM₁₀ and PM₂.₅, where 2020 and 2021 both spiked sharply above 2019 levels from August onward. This is consistent with California's record wildfire season in late 2020 and its impact spilling over onto the following year.

Figure 2. Counties with the most significant air pollution reduction during lockdown (March 19 to June 15, 2020 vs. 2019)

Figure 2 · Average % change in pollutant concentration by county · lockdown window vs. same period in 2019

Comparing each county's average pollutant concentration during the lockdown period against the same period in 2019 isolates changes related to seasonal variation. Trinity showed the largest overall reduction (average -37.7% across all pollutants), followed by Mono (-27.2%) and Mariposa (-27.1%). All 15 counties shown above recorded net reductions, with greater drops generally observed in rural counties.

Figure 3. Monthly average air pollutant concentrations: Humboldt vs. Trinity (2019 to 2021)

Figure 3 · Monthly average air pollutant concentrations · Humboldt vs. Trinity · 2019 to 2021 · crimson band = lockdown period

Trinity's 2020 pollutant levels exceeded both 2019 and 2021 across PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ despite the lockdown, with post-lockdown PM₁₀ and PM₂.₅ rising to 42.9 and 17.5 µg/m³ respectively. This was inconsistent with reduced human activity as the sole driver and was more likely attributable to California's largest wildfire season in late 2020, given Trinity's predominantly wilderness geography. Humboldt, which borders Trinity to the west, showed a similar pattern, suggesting smoke spillover. For CO, NO₂, and O₃, both counties returned closer to 2019 levels by 2021.

03 / Discussion

Why Trinity?

Trinity is one of California's least populated counties, with a total population of 16,112, ranking 54th (of 58 total) most populated county in California. In terms of land size, Trinity covers a total area of 3,208 square miles, of which 3,179 (99.1%) square miles is land, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. While Trinity is physically sizeable, it is nearly empty with only 5 people per square mile (one of the emptiest counties in the state) compared to California's overall figure of roughly 250. It is, therefore, not entirely surprising that the least populated county showed the most significant improvement in air quality during the lockdown period.

However, Trinity's 2020 air pollutant levels surpassed those of 2019 and 2021, specifically PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ levels, despite lockdown. PM₁₀ and PM₂.₅ levels rose to 42.934 and 17.526 µg/m³ post-lockdown, respectively. This significant increase is unlikely due to human activity returning to normal alone, and is more likely linked to the record-breaking California wildfire season in late 2020, given that Trinity is mostly wilderness.

04 / Limitations

Limitations

  • PM₂.₅ was consistently recorded in Trinity in comparison to other counties. Such imbalance in data collection may result in skewness. A suggestion for reproducing this analysis is to set a threshold for which counties are to be included (e.g. a minimum of 4 or 5 air pollutants must be recorded for a county to be included in the analysis).
